speaker: ALEX
text: Welcome back. Today we're getting oriented inside your personal practice space on GitHub. Think of this as your workshop sandbox, but a very real one. It has issues, branches, pull requests, automation, and review workflows, just like a live project.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So this is not just a demo repo somebody is showing on screen. It's my own working repository.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. When you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment, GitHub creates a private copy of the workshop template just for you. The template lives in Community-Access slash learning-room-template, but you do not work in that template directly. GitHub Classroom copies it into the workshop organization and names it something like learning-room-your-username.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And that copy is mine to experiment in.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. You get write access, your own branches, your own pull requests, and your own automated bot feedback. Other students are working through the same challenge sequence, but they are doing it in their own private copies. You generally won't see their work in your repo, and they won't see yours, unless facilitators intentionally pair people for review.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That privacy matters. Especially if someone is learning all of this for the first time.

speaker: ALEX
text: It does. And the workshop setup is already managed for you. You do not need to create an organization, change permissions, or wire up GitHub Actions. Facilitators handle the classroom organization, the template, the assignment, and the automation permissions.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Why give every student a separate repository instead of putting everyone into one shared practice repo?

speaker: ALEX
text: Three big reasons. Safety, authenticity, and pace. Safety means you can try things, make mistakes, and recover without affecting anyone else. Authenticity means the workflow is real: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, merging. And pace means you can move as quickly or as slowly as you need through the Day 1 challenges without blocking another learner or waiting on them.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So this is rehearsal for open source work, but with guardrails.

speaker: ALEX
text: That's a great way to say it. On Day 2, and in some bonus work, you'll contribute in a more shared setting. The Learning Room is where you build the muscle memory first: issue, branch, pull request, review, merge.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's walk through getting into it, because that first entry point can feel intimidating.

speaker: ALEX
text: Absolutely. Before you start, you need two things. First, a GitHub account, already signed into your browser. Second, the Day 1 GitHub Classroom assignment link from the facilitator. It usually looks like classroom dot github dot com slash a slash some random ID.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if I don't have that link, I should ask in chat or message a facilitator.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Once you open the assignment link in the same browser where you're signed into GitHub, the page is hosted on classroom dot github dot com. Your screen reader should announce a heading with the assignment name, something like the workshop name and Day 1.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And sometimes GitHub Classroom asks for authorization first, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. If you're prompted to authorize GitHub Classroom to access your GitHub account, activate the authorize button. That's usually a one-time step.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then there's sometimes a roster page.

speaker: ALEX
text: Correct. GitHub Classroom may ask you to identify yourself from a roster so facilitators can match your GitHub username to the registration list. If that page appears, move through the list with arrow keys, or use Find in Page, Control F on Windows or Command F on Mac, to search for your name. Activate the link or button next to it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if my name isn't there?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the Skip to the next step link, if it's available, and tell the facilitator in chat. They can reconcile the roster later. The important thing is that your repository still gets created.

speaker: ALEX
text: Next comes the main acceptance step. Activate the button that says Accept this assignment, or Accept the assignment.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What happens behind the scenes there?

speaker: ALEX
text: GitHub Classroom starts copying the learning room template into the workshop organization and granting you access to your private copy. You'll usually land on a status page that says something like, you are ready to go, with a refresh option. This process often takes ten to thirty seconds.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And I should keep refreshing until the repository link appears.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Every fifteen seconds or so, activate Refresh or reload the page with F5. The finished link will look like github dot com slash workshop-org slash learning-room-your-username.

speaker: JAMIE
text: There was also an important screen reader tip in the reading.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. The status page does not reliably auto-announce when the repository is ready. So if you use a screen reader, switch to browse mode and press K to move by links until you hear your repository link, or just keep refreshing until it appears.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Once I open the repo, what should I verify?

speaker: ALEX
text: Three things. First, the repository heading should match learning-room-your-username. Second, the About area or description should make it clear this is your private workshop copy. Third, you should see template content already there, such as folders like docs and dot github, plus files like README dot md.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And bookmark it.

speaker: ALEX
text: Definitely bookmark it. You'll return to this repository throughout Day 1.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now the first real action inside the repo: finding the first challenge issue.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Once your Learning Room is ready, Challenge 1 should appear as a GitHub issue. Facilitators use the Student Progression Bot to prepare that sequence, and later challenges unlock one at a time as you complete earlier ones.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So from the repository page, I go to Issues.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. You can use the Issues tab, or GitHub's keyboard shortcut G then I. Look for an open issue with a title like Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around. The author may be aria-bot or github-actions bot. Open it and read the issue body carefully. It tells you what to do, where to find the evidence, and how to submit completion.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if Challenge 1 isn't there yet?

speaker: ALEX
text: If it's still missing after about two minutes, refresh the Issues tab once. If it still doesn't appear, open the Actions tab and check whether the Student Progression Bot workflow ran successfully. If it failed, or never ran, post your repo link in workshop chat. A facilitator can trigger student-progression dot yml or create Challenge 1 from the issue template.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And then there's Gandalf.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes, the PR validation bot. To confirm Gandalf can talk to you, open the Actions tab and look for a workflow named pr-validation-bot or Gandalf PR Validation. You don't need to run anything yet. You're just checking that the workflow exists in your repository before you start making pull requests.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So by that point, Block 0 is really complete: repo created, first issue present or troubleshootable, automation visible.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: ALEX
text: This part of the workshop is orientation, not a challenge chapter. There are no challenge completions to submit here and no automation checks to pass yet. The purpose is to help you understand the system before the issue-based work begins.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So what should a learner be able to do before moving on?

speaker: ALEX
text: Three readiness checks. One, find docs slash CHALLENGES dot md in the repository. Two, explain the basic workflow: issue to branch to pull request to review to merge. Three, identify where Gandalf bot feedback appears on a pull request, which is the Conversation tab.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The chapter also described two learning tracks happening at the same time. That seems important, because people may confuse them.

speaker: ALEX
text: Very important. Throughout Day 1, you may be working in two related but different tracks under your own GitHub account. Track 1 is GitHub Skills modules. These are optional, self-paced exercises from GitHub, such as Introduction to GitHub, Communicate Using Markdown, and Review Pull Requests.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That's the path where GitHub's learning bot, Mona, guides you step by step.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. The scope there is your personal account, and the purpose is focused practice on individual skills like creating a branch, writing Markdown, or reviewing a PR.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And Track 2 is the required workshop track inside the Learning Room.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. That's where your Day 1 challenge sequence lives. The reading described it as blocks across the day, with challenges that include getting oriented, filing an issue, creating a branch, committing, opening a pull request, handling merge conflict practice, and then later community and merge-focused work, plus community tools like labels, milestones, and notifications.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the tracks reinforce each other, but they are not the same thing.

speaker: ALEX
text: Precisely. One is optional self-paced skills practice. The other is the required workshop experience. They use the same GitHub account, but different repositories, different bots, and different goals.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That sounds like a good learning card summary: two tracks, one account.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly that. If you ever feel confused, ask yourself: am I in a GitHub Skills training repo, or am I in my private Learning Room repo for the workshop?

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's talk about the repository layout. Even if we don't list every file on air, learners need a mental map.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Your Learning Room has a deliberate folder structure. You'll commonly encounter the docs folder, which holds most of the practice content and challenge materials. You'll also see dot github, which contains automation-related files such as workflows and issue or pull request templates. And you'll see top-level files like README dot md.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So when someone is browsing with a screen reader or keyboard, it helps to know what kinds of places they're looking for.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. The docs folder is where much of your reading and editing work happens. The dot github folder tends to support the automation and workflow side of the experience.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now let's talk branches, because this is where many beginners freeze. What is the practice branch for?

speaker: ALEX
text: Your practice branch is the branch you create to do challenge work without editing the default branch directly. The reason for a separate branch is simple but foundational: it gives you an isolated workspace for changes, makes pull requests possible, preserves a clean main branch, and mirrors real collaboration patterns used in open source projects.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So even though this is my own repo, I still use a branch because I'm practicing the real workflow.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. The branch is not about distrust. It's about process. Open the issue, create or switch to your practice branch, make the changes there, commit them, and then open a pull request back into the default branch.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if I leave and come back later?

speaker: ALEX
text: You need to make sure you're on the correct branch before editing. That's part of the tool-card idea here: know how to switch to your practice branch in whichever interface you're using, whether on the GitHub website or in VS Code. Branch awareness prevents a lot of confusion.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the branch learning card is really: use a separate branch on purpose, and return to it consciously.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The chapter also pointed to specific practice files. Let's walk through what learners will actually work on.

speaker: ALEX
text: One important file is docs slash welcome dot md. That file introduces open source contribution ideas. It includes at least three targeted to-do areas.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The first is a section about who can contribute.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. That reinforces a crucial idea: open source contribution is not limited to expert programmers. People contribute documentation, testing, bug reports, accessibility feedback, design suggestions, issue triage, community support, and many other forms of labor.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That's especially important in an accessibility-centered workshop, because contribution includes making things more usable and more inclusive.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. The second to-do area is about finding something to work on. That usually means learning how contributors identify tasks through issues, labels, documentation gaps, or starter-friendly opportunities.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So not just waiting to be told what to do, but learning how work is discovered.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. And the third to-do area is about what happens after your contribution is merged. That helps normalize that merging is not the end of the story. There may be follow-up discussion, more contributions, maintenance, and continued community participation.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That's a healthy expectation to set early.

speaker: ALEX
text: It is.

speaker: ALEX
text: Another practice file is docs slash keyboard-shortcuts dot md, a screen reader shortcut reference.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That sounds especially relevant to this audience.

speaker: ALEX
text: Very much so. It gives learners a place to practice and document useful commands they'll rely on when navigating GitHub, reading pages efficiently, moving among controls, and working confidently with keyboard and screen reader tools.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And there's docs slash setup-guide dot md.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. That file is about getting ready to contribute. It supports the practical setup mindset: before contribution comes preparation. That can include understanding tools, account readiness, navigation habits, and the basic workflow expectations that help you succeed once challenges start.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And then docs slash CHALLENGES dot md is the menu.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Think of that file as your challenge roadmap. It helps you see what kinds of tasks exist in the Learning Room, even though progression may unlock step by step through issues.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And there are bonus challenges too.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Bonus challenges let learners go further once required work is complete or when they want extra practice. They're useful for stretching skills without making the core pathway overwhelming.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now for one of the most important pieces conceptually: how pull request sharing works in this learning environment.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. The chapter laid this out as a sequence. First, the student opens a pull request.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So imagine Student A is working on Challenge 3, maybe completing part of the welcome guide.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. They make changes on their branch, then open a PR into the repository's main branch. That PR becomes the central place where the work is discussed, checked, and eventually merged.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then automation validates it.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Step 2 is the automation bot. A workflow such as dot github slash workflows slash learning-room-pr-bot dot yml, along with the validation system called Gandalf, checks the PR and posts educational feedback. This usually verifies structure or expected evidence, and helps the learner understand what is correct or what still needs attention.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the bot isn't just policing. It's teaching.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then comes peer review, but it's facilitator-arranged.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. That is an important nuance. Step 3 is not a free-for-all where everyone sees everyone's work by default. Review access is intentionally arranged. Visibility depends on how the workshop is configured. A facilitator may pair students so one learner can review another learner's PR.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then Step 4 is the reviewer reading and commenting.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. If you are assigned as a peer reviewer, you read the PR carefully, inspect the changed files, and leave comments or a formal review. Again, visibility is controlled. You review what you have been given access to review, not the entire classroom's work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then the author responds and updates.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Step 5 is where the PR author reads the feedback, replies if needed, updates their branch, and pushes new commits. The PR updates in place. This is one of the best parts of learning GitHub, because it shows that feedback is part of the workflow, not a sign of failure.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And Step 6 is merge and celebration.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Once the review is approved, or in some cases when you decide to self-merge according to workshop rules, the PR is merged. Then the progression bot can post the next challenge. That merge event is not just an ending. It also triggers progress tracking and unlocks what comes next.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the learning card summary would be: open PR, bot checks, peer review if assigned, revise, merge, next challenge unlocks.

speaker: ALEX
text: Beautifully said.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's make the visibility model extra clear. What do you see, and what do your peers see?

speaker: ALEX
text: In general, you primarily see your own private Learning Room repository: your issues, your branches, your pull requests, your bot feedback. Other students are in parallel private repos. They do not automatically browse your work, and you do not automatically browse theirs. If the workshop sets up intentional peer review, then specific access is granted for that purpose.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That means learners should not assume either extreme. Not fully public, not magical isolation from all collaboration.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. It is private by default, with structured collaboration where appropriate.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The automation system itself had three types of feedback, and that timing matters.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Type 1 is automated bot feedback, often around thirty seconds. That is your near-immediate signal after opening or updating a PR. Type 2 is peer reviewer feedback, which may take fifteen to sixty minutes depending on workshop pacing and facilitator pairing. Type 3 is progress tracking on merge, where the system recognizes that a challenge was completed and may unlock or post the next one.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That timing helps learners manage anxiety. If nothing happens in ten seconds, it doesn't mean the whole system is broken.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Know which feedback channel you're waiting for.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The reading also mentioned optional study groups.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Study groups are optional. They can help learners compare approaches, talk through concepts, or encourage one another. But they do not replace your own repository workflow. Even if you work alongside a partner or small group, each learner still needs to complete their own work in their own Learning Room unless facilitators say otherwise.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So collaboration is allowed, but ownership of the actual repo work stays individual.

speaker: ALEX
text: Correct. The example idea there is learning together while still submitting your own contribution path.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Can we sharpen the difference between a GitHub Skills module and the Learning Room one more time?

speaker: ALEX
text: Certainly. In a GitHub Skills module, the environment is a training repo, the guide is usually Mona, and the lesson is narrowly structured around one skill. In the Learning Room, the environment is your private workshop repository, the guidance comes from workshop issues, bots, documentation, and facilitators, and the goal is integrated practice across a realistic contribution workflow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So a Skills module might teach one isolated move, while the Learning Room teaches how the moves connect.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now let's talk about reviewing a peer's pull request, because learners often know how to ask for feedback before they know how to give it.

speaker: ALEX
text: A few practical tips. First, finding PRs to review. In this workshop, that often means using the link or access a facilitator provides, rather than browsing a public queue. Once you have the PR, open it and orient yourself to the Conversation tab, the Files changed tab, and any bot feedback already posted.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then reading the PR you're assigned to.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Start with the PR description. Understand what challenge the author was trying to complete. Then inspect the changed files with curiosity and care. Ask: does the change meet the stated goal, and is it clear, respectful, and complete?

speaker: JAMIE
text: What makes a good review comment?

speaker: ALEX
text: A good review is specific, actionable, and kind. Point to a concrete line or idea. Say what works well when something is strong. If something needs revision, explain why and suggest a next step. Avoid vague comments like "fix this."

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if I'm the author responding to feedback?

speaker: ALEX
text: Read generously. Ask clarifying questions if needed. Make updates on your branch, push them, and reply in the PR so the reviewer knows what changed. You do not need to treat feedback as personal criticism. It is part of collaborative improvement.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That sounds like the PR sharing learning card in plain language: locate the PR, read with context, leave kind specific comments, and respond constructively.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's run through the FAQ-style concerns, because these are the questions people often hesitate to ask aloud.

speaker: ALEX
text: Great idea.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Can I see other students' PRs?

speaker: ALEX
text: Usually not by default. Access is generally limited to your own repository unless facilitators arrange visibility for peer review or another workshop purpose.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if I don't agree with my assigned reviewer?

speaker: ALEX
text: Treat that as a conversation, not a conflict. Ask clarifying questions, explain your reasoning respectfully, and involve a facilitator if needed. Review comments are part of learning, and not every disagreement is a problem.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Will my PR get lost when everyone is working at once?

speaker: ALEX
text: Not if the workflow is functioning normally. Your PR lives in your repository, with bot checks and workshop processes around it. If something seems stalled unusually long, that's when you check the relevant tabs and ask for help.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Can I comment on someone else's PR?

speaker: ALEX
text: Only when you have access and when that interaction fits workshop expectations. Don't assume broad visibility. Follow facilitator guidance.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if my reviewer doesn't respond?

speaker: ALEX
text: Wait a reasonable amount of time, remembering that peer review may take fifteen to sixty minutes or more depending on the session. Then notify a facilitator. Don't stay stuck silently.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Can I work with a friend?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can often study with a friend or discuss ideas, especially in optional study groups, but each person should still complete their own repository work unless the facilitators explicitly set up something collaborative.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How long does review take?

speaker: ALEX
text: Bot feedback may appear in about thirty seconds. Human review often takes longer, commonly fifteen to sixty minutes in the workshop model described.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if bot feedback is wrong?

speaker: ALEX
text: That can happen. Automation is helpful, not infallible. Re-read the issue and PR requirements, compare them to your work, and ask a facilitator if the bot seems incorrect. Treat the bot as a guide, not the final authority.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Do I need to complete every challenge?

speaker: ALEX
text: Follow the workshop expectations for required challenges, and use bonus challenges as extra practice where appropriate. The exact completion target can depend on pacing, but the core challenge sequence is there for a reason.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If someone gets stuck anywhere in this system, what's the advice?

speaker: ALEX
text: First, pause and identify where you are in the workflow. Are you trying to find the repo, locate an issue, switch branches, open a PR, interpret bot feedback, or wait for review? Second, check the relevant tab: Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, or the Conversation tab in the PR. Third, use the workshop chat or contact a facilitator with a specific question and, if possible, the link to the repo or PR.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So not just "it's broken," but "I'm in my Learning Room, Challenge 1 is missing," or "my PR bot feedback says something I don't understand."

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Specific context gets you help faster.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I also want to underline something emotional here. Opening issues and pull requests in a learning repo can still feel vulnerable.

speaker: ALEX
text: It can. But that's why this environment exists. You are contributing in a structured, supportive space designed for learning. Every branch you create, every issue you open, every PR you revise, every comment you leave thoughtfully, that is real contribution practice.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So even though it's a classroom setup, it is still authentic contribution behavior.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. You are learning the habits that make open source participation possible: clarity, iteration, review, and collaboration. That deserves celebration.

speaker: ALEX
text: Before we wrap, two administrative reminders from the reading. There is a podcast version of this chapter you can use before or after reading as reinforcement, and the appendices like the glossary and Markdown reference remain useful companions as you work. The chapter also pointed to authoritative GitHub documentation, especially around README files, editing files, GitHub flow, Git, and pull requests. Those are excellent references whenever you want the official version of how a feature works.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the takeaway is: get into your private Learning Room, confirm the first issue and the bots are there, understand the two-track model, use branches on purpose, work through the practice files, and expect a real pull request workflow with automation and possibly peer review.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Once that mental model clicks, the rest of Day 1 becomes much easier to navigate.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if you're listening as a blind or low-vision learner, remember that the workflow is absolutely navigable with keyboard and screen reader strategies. Use the page structure, GitHub shortcuts where they help, browse mode commands like moving by links, and don't hesitate to bookmark the key places you return to often.

speaker: ALEX
text: Beautifully said. You have your own space. You have a process. And you are ready to start contributing.
